title: Performance anti-patterns
scopeHtml:
Scope: N+1, chatty services, thundering herd, unbounded queues, lock contention, GC pauses, other anti-patterns.

Scope: N+1, chatty services, thundering herd, unbounded queues, lock contention, GC pauses, other anti-patterns.

notes.title: Why anti-patterns matter
notes.html:
A performance anti-pattern is a common design mistake that works fine in a demo and collapses under real load. Most production slowdowns are not exotic; they are a handful of repeating shapes. Learning to spot them in a design or a code review is a core senior skill.

Method for any slowness:

  1. Measure first (p50/p99 latency, throughput, CPU, memory, GC, DB time, queue depth). Do not guess.
  2. Find the bottleneck resource (USE method): CPU, memory, disk, network, locks, connection pool.
  3. Fix the cheapest big thing, measure again.

Amdahl's law reminder: if 90% of the time is in the database, making the app code 10x faster improves overall time by only about 8%.

The anti-patterns below: N+1 queries, chatty services, thundering herd (and cache stampede), unbounded queues and unbounded everything, lock contention, GC pauses, plus a short list of others.

Industry examples. Facebook's memcache paper described leases to stop thundering herds; Twitter's early Rails "fail whale" era was partly N+1 and queue problems; Discord moved a hot service from Go to Rust partly due to garbage-collection latency spikes every couple of minutes (their public write-up); LinkedIn and Netflix tuned JVM GC extensively.

Everyday analogy. A traffic jam usually has one cause (a narrow bridge); widening every other road does not help.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising without measuring.
  • Fixing symptoms (add more servers) when a code-level pattern is the cause.

notes.title: N+1 queries
notes.html:
The N+1 problem: 1 query fetches a list of N items, then N more queries fetch each item's related data one by one. Total N+1 round trips instead of 1 or 2.

// Looks innocent: 1 query for orders + N queries for each order's customer
val orders = orderRepo.findAll()                      // 1 query (say 100 rows)
orders.forEach { o -> println(o.customer.name) }      // lazy load: 100 more queries

Why it hurts. Each query costs a network round trip (0.3 to 1 ms in-region) plus parsing and planning. 100 orders -> 101 queries -> 30 to 100 ms; 10,000 rows -> over 5 seconds, and it multiplies DB load at scale: 1,000 req/s x 101 queries = 101,000 queries/s, which can saturate the database.

Fixes:

  • Join / join fetch: one query: SELECT ... FROM orders JOIN customers. JPA: JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph.
  • Batch fetch (IN query): SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id IN (...), 2 queries total; Hibernate @BatchSize, or Rails includes/preload, Django select_related / prefetch_related.
  • DataLoader (GraphQL): batches and caches per-request loads (Facebook's DataLoader).
  • Denormalise or cache rarely-changing related data.
  • Android Room: use @Relation with @Transaction rather than querying inside a loop.
-- 1 query instead of 101
SELECT o.id, o.total, c.name
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.created_at > now() - interval '1 day';

-- or 2 queries
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ...;
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id IN (7, 9, 12, 15);

Detection. Log or count SQL statements per request (Hibernate statistics, pg_stat_statements showing one query with huge call counts and tiny mean time), APM traces showing hundreds of identical sibling DB spans, tests that assert query counts (Django assertNumQueries).

Trade-offs. A big join can return duplicated parent data (one-to-many cartesian explosion): use batched IN queries or fetch separately. Over-fetching columns also costs memory.

Decision gravity. Easy to fix locally and reversible; the real fix is a team habit: query-count assertions in tests and ORM lazy-loading awareness.

Industry examples. GitHub's GraphQL API and Shopify use DataLoader-style batching; Rails's Bullet gem flags N+1; Hibernate lazy loading is the classic cause.

Everyday analogy. Going to the supermarket 100 times to buy 100 items instead of making one trip with a list.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing an ORM makes this go away.
  • "Fixing" it with a huge join that returns millions of duplicated rows.
  • Not checking the SQL the ORM actually generated.

notes.title: Chatty services
notes.html:
A chatty service makes many small remote calls to do one job. Each call adds latency (network RTT plus serialization) and failure probability.

In-process call: nanoseconds. Cross-service call in the same datacenter: about 0.5 to 2 ms plus the callee's time. Calls multiply: a page that makes 40 sequential calls of 5 ms each is 200 ms before any logic.

Availability also multiplies: 40 calls each 99.9% -> 0.999^40 = 96%.

Fixes:

  • Batching: one call with a list of IDs instead of N calls (GET /users?ids=1,2,3).
  • Parallelise independent calls (async/await, coroutines async), so latency is the max not the sum.
  • Coarser-grained APIs: return what the screen needs (BFF: Backend For Frontend, GraphQL, or an aggregated endpoint).
  • Caching stable data near the caller.
  • Co-locate tightly coupled logic (merge services if two always change and scale together; the "distributed monolith" smell).
  • Use async messaging for work that does not need a response.
  • Efficient protocols: gRPC/protobuf and HTTP/2 multiplexing, keep-alive connections.
// Kotlin: independent calls in parallel -> latency = max(a,b,c), not a+b+c
suspend fun home(userId: String) = coroutineScope {
    val profile = async { profileApi.get(userId) }
    val orders  = async { orderApi.recent(userId) }
    val recs    = async { recsApi.forUser(userId) }
    HomeScreen(profile.await(), orders.await(), recs.await())
}

Worked example. Mobile home screen: 12 sequential REST calls at 80 ms (mobile network RTT) = 960 ms plus TLS handshakes if not reused. A BFF that fans out in parallel in the datacenter (12 calls at 3 ms, in parallel, about 10 ms) returns one response in about 100 ms total to the phone. Mobile benefits hugely because the expensive hop is the radio link.

Industry examples. Netflix's API gateway/BFF and later GraphQL federation reduce device round trips; Amazon's famous page assembled from many services with strict per-call latency budgets; Uber reorganised from thousands of microservices toward domain-oriented boundaries (DOMA) partly to reduce chatty dependencies; Amazon Prime Video moved a monitoring pipeline from microservices to a monolith and cut cost by 90% (their 2023 write-up).

Decision gravity. Service boundaries are close to one-way doors: merging or splitting services is expensive. Draw boundaries along data ownership and change cadence so that typical operations stay within one service.

Everyday analogy. Asking a colleague 20 separate one-line questions by email instead of sending one message with all 20.

Common interview traps.

  • Sequential calls that could be parallel.
  • Calling a service in a loop (the N+1 problem across the network).
  • Splitting into microservices without considering call graphs.

notes.title: Thundering herd and cache stampede
notes.html:
A thundering herd is many clients or threads reacting to the same event at the same instant, overwhelming a shared resource. Typical triggers: a popular cache key expires, a service restarts, a lock is released, a cron fires at :00, a push notification wakes millions of devices.

Cache stampede (dogpile). A hot key expires; 5,000 requests/s all miss at once and all hit the database to recompute it. The DB, sized for a 95% cache hit rate, suddenly gets 100% of traffic and falls over, which in turn keeps the cache from refilling.

Fixes:

  1. Request coalescing / single flight: only one request recomputes; others wait for its result (Go singleflight, Guava LoadingCache, Caffeine refreshAfterWrite).
  2. Distributed lock or lease on the key (Facebook memcache "leases": one client gets a lease to refill; others wait or get a slightly stale value).
  3. Stale-while-revalidate / serve stale on error: keep returning the old value while one refresher updates it in the background.
  4. TTL jitter: TTL = 300 s + random(0, 60 s) so many keys do not expire together.
  5. Probabilistic early refresh (XFetch): refresh with increasing probability as expiry approaches.
  6. Pre-warming caches before taking traffic after a deploy or failover.
  7. Never expire extremely hot keys, refresh them by a background job.
import random, time

def ttl_with_jitter(base=300, spread=60):
    return base + random.uniform(0, spread)       # avoid synchronised expiry

# Single-flight idea: first caller computes, others wait on the same future
inflight = {}
def get(key):
    v = cache.get(key)
    if v is not None:
        return v
    fut = inflight.setdefault(key, new_future())   # only the first creates the work
    if fut.is_new:
        fut.set(recompute(key)); cache.set(key, fut.value, ttl_with_jitter())
    return fut.wait()

Other herds.

  • Retry storms after an outage (use backoff and jitter).
  • Reconnect storms: a WebSocket gateway restarts and 2M mobile clients reconnect in seconds. Use randomised reconnect delays, connection rate limits and gradual rollouts.
  • Cron at midnight: spread schedules with jitter. Android WorkManager and Firebase push both batch and jitter to avoid server spikes.
  • Cold start after failover: empty caches mean 100% misses.

Worked example. Key with 10,000 req/s, DB recompute takes 200 ms. Without coalescing, during those 200 ms about 2,000 requests each run the expensive query. With single flight, exactly 1 query runs and 1,999 requests share the result.

Industry examples. Facebook's memcache leases (NSDI 2013 paper); Cloudflare and Fastly "request collapsing" to the origin; Varnish grace mode; Netflix EVCache; Instagram.

Decision gravity. Cheap to add early (jitter, single flight) and reversible; painful to discover during an outage. Stale-serving is a product decision: which data may be stale and for how long.

Everyday analogy. The shop opens its doors at 9:00 on sale day and everyone rushes the one till; staggered entry or several tills fixes it.

Common interview traps.

  • All keys sharing the same TTL.
  • Fixing the cache stampede but leaving retry storms and reconnect storms.
  • Not warming caches on a new region or after a flush.

notes.title: Unbounded queues and unbounded everything
notes.html:
Anything without a limit will eventually grow until it breaks something else. Unbounded queues, thread pools, caches, result sets, retries, request sizes and connection counts.

The unbounded queue. When arrival rate > service rate, a queue absorbs the difference only while memory lasts. Latency becomes (queue length / service rate): a backlog of 600,000 items at 1,000 items/s means 10 minutes wait, so every request is already stale and users have retried. Then OOM kills the process and the queue is lost.

Classic traps:

  • Java Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue; newCachedThreadPool has unbounded threads. Create ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue and a rejection policy (CallerRunsPolicy applies backpressure).
  • Unbounded in-memory caches (HashMap as cache): use Caffeine with maximumSize and TTL.
  • SELECT * without LIMIT/pagination loading millions of rows into memory.
  • Unbounded retry loops and log volume (disk fills).
  • Unbounded per-tenant usage (no quotas): one tenant starves others.
  • Android: unbounded in-memory bitmap caches cause OOM; use LruCache sized as a fraction of heap.
// Bounded pool: 16 threads, queue of 200, caller runs when full (natural backpressure)
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    16, 16, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(200),
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());

Worked example. Queue holds 1 KB messages. A 30-minute overload at +2,000 msg/s net adds 3.6M messages = 3.6 GB, enough to crash a 4 GB heap. With a bound of 10,000 messages (10 MB) the system rejects the excess immediately and stays alive.

Little's law check. In-flight items = arrival rate x time in system. 1,000 req/s at 2 s latency means 2,000 concurrent requests holding resources; if latency rises to 20 s this becomes 20,000: memory and threads explode. Bound concurrency, and monitor queue depth and queue wait time.

Choose the overflow policy explicitly: block producers, reject (503), drop oldest/newest (telemetry), or spill to durable storage (Kafka, SQS).

Industry examples. Many JVM incidents trace back to newFixedThreadPool; Kafka and SQS act as durable bounded-by-disk buffers with lag alerts; Netflix concurrency limits; Slack's 2021 outage retrospectives mention overload and scaling limits (confirm details in their post-mortems).

Decision gravity. Choosing bounds and overflow behaviour is a design-time decision, easy to change, but defaults are dangerous. Persistent queues change durability guarantees (at-least-once, ordering).

Everyday analogy. A bathtub with the tap on full and a drain that is too small: without an overflow outlet, it floods the house.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "add a queue" to absorb load without bounding it.
  • Using default executors.
  • Monitoring CPU but not queue depth/age.

notes.title: Lock contention
notes.html:
Lock contention is threads spending their time waiting for a lock instead of working. Adding CPUs or threads makes it no faster, sometimes slower.

Symptoms: low CPU utilisation but poor throughput and high latency; thread dumps show many threads BLOCKED or WAITING on the same monitor; throughput plateaus as you add threads. In databases: lock waits (pg_locks with granted = false), row-lock hot spots, deadlocks.

Amdahl: if 10% of the work happens inside one global lock (serial), the maximum speed-up is 1 / 0.10 = 10x, no matter how many cores.

Fixes:

  • Shorten the critical section: do I/O, logging and computation outside the lock.
  • Reduce granularity: per-key/striped locks (ConcurrentHashMap locks per bin / CAS), sharded counters (LongAdder rather than a single AtomicLong under heavy contention).
  • Lock-free / immutable data: copy-on-write for read-mostly data (CopyOnWriteArrayList), ReadWriteLock / StampedLock when reads dominate.
  • Avoid lock ordering deadlocks: always acquire in a consistent order, use tryLock with timeout.
  • Message passing / single writer: one thread owns the data (actor model, LMAX Disruptor, Kotlin channels), eliminating locks.
  • Database hot rows: counter on one row updated by every request. Fix with sharded counters (N rows, sum on read), batching/aggregation in memory, INSERT event rows and aggregate later, or Redis INCR. Keep transactions short; take locks in the same order; SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for queues.
// Bad: synchronized around a slow call
@Synchronized fun update(x: Item) { db.save(x); cache.put(x.id, x) }   // db.save under the lock

// Better: do slow work outside, lock only the tiny shared update
fun update(x: Item) { db.save(x); synchronized(lock) { cache[x.id] = x } }
-- Hot row: every order updates one counter row (serialises all writers)
UPDATE stats SET orders = orders + 1 WHERE id = 1;
-- Sharded: pick random slot of 16; sum on read
UPDATE stats_sharded SET orders = orders + 1 WHERE id = floor(random()*16);

Worked example. A service guards a map with one synchronized block that takes 2 ms (includes a log call). Max throughput = 1 / 0.002 = 500 ops/s, regardless of 32 cores. Moving logging out (0.05 ms inside the lock) gives 20,000 ops/s.

Diagnosis tools. JVM: thread dumps (jstack, 3 dumps 5 s apart), async-profiler lock mode, JFR lock profiling; Linux perf, off-CPU flame graphs; Postgres pg_stat_activity wait_event, pg_locks; MySQL performance_schema/InnoDB status.

Industry examples. LMAX Disruptor (single writer, lock-free ring buffer) for trading; Java's LongAdder born from this; Instagram/Twitter counters sharded; Kafka and Redis single-threaded event loops avoid locks by design (Redis executes commands on one thread).

Decision gravity. Choosing a concurrency model (shared state with locks vs single-writer/actors) is a deep design choice, hard to change later; reducing lock scope inside code is cheap and reversible.

Everyday analogy. A single toilet in an office: more employees do not make the queue shorter; more toilets (finer granularity) do.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding threads to a lock-bound system.
  • Holding a lock across network or disk I/O.
  • A single global counter or row updated by every request.
  • Inconsistent lock ordering (deadlock).

notes.title: GC pauses and memory pressure
notes.html:
Garbage collection (GC) reclaims unused memory automatically, but some phases stop the application (stop-the-world, STW). Long pauses show up as latency spikes, timeouts, and failed health checks.

Why it matters at senior level: a 3-second pause makes a node look dead (missed heartbeats, lock lease expiry, failover, load balancer ejection), which can cascade into split brain or retry storms.

Rough JVM picture (confirm per version):

  • Young generation collections are frequent and short (milliseconds).
  • Old generation / full GC can be long with big heaps and the older collectors (seconds).
  • G1 (default since Java 9) targets a pause goal (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200); ZGC and Shenandoah aim for sub-millisecond to few-millisecond pauses largely independent of heap size (ZGC generational mode added in newer JDKs). Pick a modern collector for latency-sensitive services.
  • Allocation rate drives GC frequency: allocating 1 GB/s with a 2 GB young gen means a young GC every couple of seconds.

Common causes and fixes:

  • High allocation rate: reduce garbage (avoid boxing, string concatenation in loops, large temporary lists, JSON parsing copies); reuse buffers; object pools only when profiling proves it.
  • Heap too small (constant GC) or too large with old collector (long full GC).
  • Memory leak: unbounded cache/static map/listener never removed: the old generation fills, full GCs become back-to-back, throughput collapses ("GC death spiral" where the JVM spends >98% time in GC and throws OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded).
  • Large humongous allocations in G1 (objects over half a region).
  • Container limits: JVM heap + metaspace + threads + native memory exceed the pod's memory limit and the OOM killer ends the process (use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70; confirm flags for your JDK).
  • Safepoint pauses and swap activity (never swap a JVM).
# JVM flags often used for a latency-sensitive service (illustrative, tune with measurements)
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms4g -Xmx4g -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime \
     -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -jar app.jar

Detection. GC logs (-Xlog:gc*), JFR, metrics like jvm_gc_pause_seconds, heap usage after GC trending upward (leak), p99 latency spikes aligned with GC events; heap dumps (Eclipse MAT) to find leaks.

Android angle. ART's GC is concurrent but allocation-heavy code in onDraw, scrolling lists or per-frame objects causes jank (dropped frames, 16 ms budget at 60 Hz). Fixes: avoid allocations in hot UI paths, reuse objects, use RecyclerView view recycling, profile with Android Studio Memory Profiler, watch for leaked Activities (static references, listeners).

Worked example. Service with a 16 GB heap on old Parallel GC sees a 4 s full GC every 30 minutes; the load balancer health check times out at 3 s and removes the node, then all nodes do it around the same time. Moving to G1/ZGC with a 6 GB heap and fixing a 2 KB-per-request garbage source reduces pauses to under 20 ms.

Industry examples. Discord (Go to Rust for Read States service due to GC spikes), Twitter (tuning JVM, Finagle), LinkedIn, Netflix (JVM tuning with G1/ZGC), Cassandra (historically GC-sensitive, community moved to G1/ZGC), Elasticsearch (heap capped near 30 GB to keep compressed object pointers).

Decision gravity. Collector choice and heap sizing are reversible flags. Moving language/runtime (JVM to Rust/C++) is a one-way door chosen only for extreme latency or memory needs. Make sure heartbeat timeouts exceed realistic pauses.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant that stops serving for a few minutes while staff clear all tables at once: customers notice, and the longer the break, the angrier they are.

Common interview traps.

  • "Just give it more heap": larger heap with a pausing collector means longer pauses.
  • Treating GC as a magic detail instead of a source of latency spikes and false failure detection.
  • Setting health-check or lease timeouts shorter than the worst GC pause.

notes.title: Other common anti-patterns and a checklist
notes.html:
Short list worth recognising:

Anti-pattern Symptom Fix
Missing index / full table scan Query time grows with table size, DB CPU high EXPLAIN ANALYZE, add the right composite index
Over-fetching (SELECT *, huge payloads) High bandwidth, memory Select needed columns, paginate, compress
Offset pagination on big tables Page 10,000 is slow (OFFSET 1000000) Keyset (seek) pagination WHERE id > :last ORDER BY id LIMIT 50
Synchronous work in the request path High latency tails Move email, thumbnails, analytics to async queue
Connection per request TLS and connection setup cost, DB max connections Connection pools, keep-alive, HTTP/2, PgBouncer
Hot partition / hot key One shard at 100%, others idle Better key, salting, split hot key, local cache
Serial processing of independent work Latency = sum Parallelise within limits
No caching of expensive pure results Repeated identical computation Cache with TTL, invalidate carefully
Premature or wrong microservices Chatty calls, distributed monolith Fewer, domain-aligned services
Logging/serialization on the hot path CPU in JSON/log frameworks Async logging, sampling, binary formats

Quick checklist for design reviews:

  1. Any loop that makes a DB or network call per item?
  2. Any queue, pool, cache or result set without a bound?
  3. Any hot key, hot row or single global lock?
  4. Do all remote calls have timeouts, and are retries jittered and budgeted?
  5. What happens when the cache is cold or a key expires?
  6. What are GC/pause and heartbeat timeouts relative to each other?
  7. Which metrics (p99, queue depth, lock wait, GC pause) will tell us?

Worked example. Keyset vs offset pagination: OFFSET 1,000,000 LIMIT 50 makes Postgres read and discard 1M rows (hundreds of ms to seconds), while WHERE id > 1000000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 using the primary key index reads 50 rows (under a millisecond).

Industry examples. Slack, Stripe and GitHub APIs use cursor-based pagination for exactly this reason; Amazon DynamoDB hot-partition guidance; Instagram's early use of PgBouncer.

Common interview traps.

  • Listing anti-patterns without how you would detect them.
  • Fixing the one you know (e.g. caching) while the bottleneck is elsewhere.
  • Not stating the metric that proves the fix worked.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Measure first; find the bottleneck resource; fix the biggest one; re-measure (Amdahl: small parts of the time cannot give big wins).
  • N+1: one query per item. Use joins, batched IN queries, DataLoader, and assert query counts.
  • Chatty services: many small calls add latency and multiply failure odds. Batch, parallelise, aggregate (BFF), align boundaries to data.
  • Thundering herd and cache stampede: single flight, locks/leases, stale-while-revalidate, TTL jitter, warm caches; also retry and reconnect storms.
  • Unbounded queues, pools, caches and result sets turn overload into OOM and huge latency. Bound everything and choose an overflow policy.
  • Lock contention: low CPU but poor throughput. Shorten critical sections, shard, use lock-free or single-writer designs; beware hot DB rows and keyset vs offset pagination.
  • GC pauses cause latency spikes and false failure detection; pick a suitable collector, reduce allocation, fix leaks, and keep timeouts above worst-case pauses.

questions.promptHtml: What is the N+1 query problem, why does it hurt, and how do you fix and detect it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most common ORM performance bug; the answer shows whether you look at the SQL your code generates.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One query loads a list of N items, then the code issues one more query per item for related data, so N+1 round trips instead of 1 or 2. Each round trip costs 0.3 to 1 ms plus parse and plan, so 100 orders is 101 queries, and at 1,000 req/s that is 101,000 queries/s on the database. I fix it with a join or join fetch, or a batched IN query (2 queries total), or a DataLoader in GraphQL. I detect it by counting SQL per request: Hibernate statistics, pg_stat_statements showing one statement with a huge call count and a tiny mean time, APM traces with hundreds of identical sibling DB spans, and tests that assert query counts.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Cause: lazy loading in a loop (order.customer triggers a query).
  • Join returns one row per child; a one-to-many join can duplicate parent data, so for large collections use a second batched query (WHERE id IN (...), Hibernate @BatchSize, Django prefetch_related).
-- 1 query instead of 101
SELECT o.id, o.total, c.name
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.created_at > now() - interval '1 day';

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
List<Order> orders = em.createQuery(
    "select o from Order o join fetch o.customer", Order.class).getResultList();
val orders = em.createQuery(
    "select o from Order o join fetch o.customer", Order::class.java).resultList

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing an ORM makes the problem disappear.
  • A huge join that returns millions of duplicated rows.
  • Never looking at the generated SQL.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Join vs IN query? -> Join for to-one relations; separate IN query for large to-many to avoid row duplication.
  2. How would a test catch it? -> Assert the number of statements per request (Django assertNumQueries, Hibernate statistics).
  3. Does GraphQL have it? -> Yes, per field resolver; DataLoader batches per request.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "use join fetch". Senior shows the cost math at scale, the cartesian trade-off, and how to detect it in tracing and tests before production.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A list page that was fine in staging with 10 rows took 5 s in production with 10,000 rows and doubled DB load.

questions.promptHtml: What is a cache stampede, and what are your options to prevent it? Which do you combine?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the classic failure when a hot key expires; it tests breadth and judgement.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A hot key expires and thousands of requests miss at once and all recompute from the database. The DB was sized for a 95% hit rate and suddenly gets 100% of traffic, which keeps the cache from refilling. Fixes: single flight (only one request recomputes, the rest wait), a lock or lease on the key, serve stale while one refresher updates it, TTL jitter so keys do not expire together, probabilistic early refresh, pre-warming after deploys or failovers, and background refresh for extremely hot keys. In practice I combine jitter, single flight and stale-while-revalidate.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Math: 10,000 req/s on a key, recompute takes 200 ms: about 2,000 requests run the expensive query. With single flight, 1 query runs and 1,999 share its result.
  • Each fix covers a different gap: jitter prevents synchronised expiry, single flight limits one key, stale-serving protects when the recompute is slow or failing.
import random

def ttl_with_jitter(base=300, spread=60):
    return base + random.uniform(0, spread)   # avoid synchronised expiry

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• All keys share the same TTL.
  • Fixing the stampede but leaving retry and reconnect storms.
  • A distributed lock with no timeout on the refresher.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Single flight in a multi-node cluster? -> Per-process coalescing reduces N-requests to N-nodes; add a distributed lease for exactly one.
  2. When is stale data acceptable? -> A product decision per data type and maximum age.
  3. Cold start after failover? -> Pre-warm caches before shifting traffic; otherwise 100% misses.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "use a lock". Senior lists layered defences, does the numbers, and covers cold caches and other herds.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A top-of-page "trending" key expired at midnight under peak load and the DB was overwhelmed for 6 minutes.

questions.contextHtml:
After a release, GET /orders p99 goes from 120 ms to 2.4 s for users with many orders. DB CPU rises from 30% to 85%; app CPU is 20%. pg_stat_statements excerpt:

query                                         calls      mean_ms   total_ms
select * from customers where id = $1        4,820,000    0.38      1,831,600
select * from orders where created_at > $1      41,000    21.0        861,000

Release notes mention a new "customer name" field in the order list DTO. Another change in the same release raised the connection pool from 20 to 40 (possible red herring).
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix, and say how you stop it from coming back.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add an index on customers.id" (it is the primary key already) or "scale the DB".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the page size? Is the field lazily loaded by the ORM? Is there a feature flag for the new field?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the field via flag or roll back; if not possible, add a short-TTL cache for customer names.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: N+1 on the new field (calls ratio about 117 customer queries per orders query); pool size change (secondary); missing index (no, it is a PK lookup at 0.38 ms).
  4. How I'd verify: 4.82M calls / 41k = about 117 per request; trace shows hundreds of sibling spans; log SQL for one request.
  5. Root cause: Lazy loading of order.customer inside the DTO mapper issues one query per order. Each is fast; the total is the problem. The bigger pool just allows more concurrent queries onto the DB.
  6. Fix: join fetch or @EntityGraph for the list endpoint, or batch load customers with one IN query; select only needed columns.
  7. Prevention: Test asserting max statements per endpoint; an N+1 detector in CI; PR checklist on loops that call the repository.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise the pool again or scale the DB, which only masks the multiplication.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Customer data is in another service -> Batch API (ids=) or cache; never call per row.
  • Page size 500? -> Cap page size and use keyset pagination.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: one DTO mapper change added 100x load; fixed with a batch fetch and a statement-count test.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds index or hardware.
  • Hire: reads call counts, identifies N+1, fixes with join or batch.
  • Strong hire: ratios from stats, query-count tests, cross-service batching.

questions.contextHtml: The mobile home screen makes 12 sequential REST calls (profile, orders, recs, banners...) at 80 ms mobile RTT each, about 960 ms plus TLS setup when connections are not reused. Product wants under 300 ms to first content and will 10x traffic to 20,000 req/s next quarter. Each call is 99.9% available. The backend team proposes "make each service faster".
questions.promptHtml: Design the fix and show the numbers.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Optimising each service from 5 ms to 3 ms; the dominant cost is 12 round trips on the radio.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which calls are independent? Which data may be cached? Which fields does the screen need? Do we own a gateway?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reuse connections (HTTP/2, keep-alive) and parallelise independent calls on the client.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Sequential calls (sum not max); per-call TLS; over-fetching.
  4. How I'd verify: A trace from app to services; the waterfall shows the serial chain.
  5. Root cause: Latency is 12 x 80 ms = 960 ms; availability is 0.999^12 = 98.8%.
  6. Fix: A BFF or aggregated endpoint fans out in the datacenter in parallel (12 calls at about 3 ms, in parallel about 10 ms) and returns one response: about 100 ms total, one radio round trip. Cache stable pieces, return partial results when a non-critical call fails.
  7. Prevention: Per-screen latency budgets, a lint on sequential awaits, load tests at 20,000 req/s.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The BFF becomes a team-owned component and a possible bottleneck; service boundaries are close to one-way doors, so I would not merge services just for this. I would not parallelise without timeouts per call.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One call is slow (p99 800 ms) -> Per-call timeout and fallback or placeholders.
  • GraphQL instead? -> It solves over-fetching but needs batching (DataLoader) to avoid N+1 behind it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a screen was made of 40 sequential calls; a BFF with parallel fan-out and partial responses cut p95 from 2.5 s to 400 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes individual services.
  • Hire: BFF with parallel calls, computes latency and availability.
  • Strong hire: partial responses, timeouts, budgets per hop, boundary discussion.

questions.contextHtml:
An admin export endpoint pages through a 40M-row events table using LIMIT 50 OFFSET :n ordered by id. Page 1 takes 2 ms; page 20,000 (offset 1,000,000) takes 900 ms; scraping scripts crawl deep and DB CPU spikes. The query selects * including a 5 KB JSON column. Also, a separate query filtering WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC is doing a sequential scan.

Limit  (cost=...) (actual time=902.1..902.2 rows=50)
  ->  Index Scan using events_pkey  (actual time=0.03..851.4 rows=1000050)

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more indexes" without recognising that offset reads and discards rows.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do clients need random page access or just next/prev? Is the ordering key unique? Which columns are needed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap maximum offset and rate limit the endpoint.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Offset scans and discards 1M rows (the plan shows 1,000,050 rows read to return 50); SELECT * pulls 5 KB per row; missing composite index for the tenant query.
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on both queries.
  5. Root cause: Offset cost grows linearly with page number.
  6. Fix: Keyset pagination: WHERE id > :last ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 reads 50 rows (under a millisecond); return a cursor. Select needed columns only. Add composite index (tenant_id, created_at DESC).
  7. Prevention: Review rule: no OFFSET over large tables; query plans in CI for hot queries.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Keyset removes jump-to-page-N; for UI that needs it, cap depth or offer search. I would not cache deep pages.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Sort by a non-unique column -> Add the id as a tie-breaker in the cursor (created_at, id).
  • Total count needed -> Approximate counts or cached counts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a customer script paged to offset 5M and held DB CPU at 90%; keyset cursors fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more indexes or hardware.
  • Hire: keyset pagination, narrower columns, composite index.
  • Strong hire: tie-breaker cursors, depth caps, plan evidence.

questions.contextHtml:
During a Redis maintenance window the cache is flushed at 10:00 (peak: 8,000 req/s). Before: hit ratio 96%, DB at 400 qps. After: hit ratio 0%, DB attempts 8,000 qps and its connection pool saturates; p99 goes 90 ms to 12 s, then clients retry (retry rate 3x) and the site is down for 9 minutes even after Redis is healthy.

db_connections_in_use 200/200  waiting_threads 1,900
cache_hit_ratio 0.00   retries_total rate 24,000/s
questions.promptHtml: Explain why recovery was slow and how you would redesign.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the DB pool", which makes the DB collapse faster.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why was a flush needed at peak? Is there a read replica? Do clients back off?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load (rate limit or 503 on non-critical paths), disable client retries or add backoff, serve stale where possible, warm the hottest keys before readmitting traffic.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Cold cache stampede; retry storm amplifying; pool too large relative to DB capacity.
  4. How I'd verify: Hit ratio and DB wait metrics; retry counters.
  5. Root cause: The DB is sized for 4% of traffic. Zero cache means 20x load; timeouts caused retries that kept the load above capacity even after the cache could refill: a metastable failure.
  6. Fix: Pre-warm hot keys in the background, single-flight on misses, TTL jitter, stale-while-revalidate, client exponential backoff with jitter, retry budgets, and a rollout procedure for cache maintenance (one node at a time, off-peak).
  7. Prevention: Load-test the cold-cache case; game day; alerts on hit ratio drop.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Stale serving needs product agreement. I would not flush a cache at peak, and not enlarge the pool to match the incoming load.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• New region launch with an empty cache -> Warm from a replica or replay recent traffic; ramp gradually.
  • Why jitter on retries? -> Synchronised retries re-form the herd.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a failover to an empty standby cache triggered a stampede and a retry storm; a ramp-up weighted rollout fixed the next failover.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases pool or restarts.
  • Hire: single flight, jitter, warm cache, backoff.
  • Strong hire: names the metastable failure, retry budgets, maintenance procedure, cold-cache load test.

questions.promptHtml: Why is "just add a queue to absorb the load" dangerous? Use Little's law and name concrete unbounded things in a JVM service.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Backpressure and bounded resources separate people who have survived overload from those who have not.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A queue only absorbs the difference between arrival and service rate while memory lasts. Latency becomes queue length over service rate: a backlog of 600,000 items at 1,000 items/s is a 10-minute wait, so every item is stale and users have retried, and then the process OOMs and the queue is lost. Little's law says in-flight items = arrival rate x time in system, so 1,000 req/s at 2 s latency is 2,000 concurrent requests; if latency goes to 20 s it is 20,000, and memory and threads explode. So I bound every queue, pool and cache and choose the overflow policy explicitly: block, reject with 503, drop, or spill to a durable queue.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• JVM traps: newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue; newCachedThreadPool has unbounded threads; HashMap used as a cache; SELECT * with no LIMIT.
  • CallerRunsPolicy gives natural backpressure: when the queue is full the producer runs the task and slows down.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    16, 16, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(200),
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(
    16, 16, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
    ArrayBlockingQueue(200),
    ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy())

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Answering "add a queue" with no bound.
  • Default executors.
  • Monitoring CPU but not queue depth and queue age.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Queue holds 1 KB messages and overload adds 2,000 msg/s for 30 min? -> 3.6M messages is about 3.6 GB, enough to OOM a 4 GB heap; a bound of 10,000 is 10 MB.
  2. Block or reject? -> Reject (503 with Retry-After) at the edge, block only inside a bounded pipeline; spill to Kafka or SQS when durability matters.
  3. What metric alerts first? -> Queue wait time (age of oldest item), then depth.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "use Kafka". Senior bounds each stage, picks an overflow policy per data type and monitors queue age.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An executor with an unbounded queue held 4M tasks during a downstream slowdown and OOM-killed the pod, losing all of them.

questions.contextHtml:
An image-processing service has an in-memory LinkedBlockingQueue (default fixed pool, 32 threads). Normal arrival is 800 jobs/s, service rate 1,000/s. A downstream storage slowdown cuts service rate to 400/s for 30 minutes. Heap is 4 GB, each job is 1 KB. Metrics:

queue_depth   0 -> 1.2M -> 2.9M      p99 job latency 40 ms -> 90 s
jvm heap used 1.1 GB -> 3.9 GB       gc pause 20 ms -> 6 s (back-to-back full GC)
pod restarts: OOMKilled x3

Clients retry after 10 s timeouts. CPU is at 35%.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what happened, the immediate mitigation, and the redesign.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more memory and more consumers." The service rate was limited by storage, not by consumers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can jobs be dropped or must they be durable? Does the client need a synchronous answer? Are jobs idempotent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load at the edge (503 with Retry-After), stop client retries, scale storage or the slow dependency; do not restart blindly since each restart drops the queue.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Arrival 800/s > service 400/s net +400/s; unbounded queue; retries adding load; GC death spiral as heap fills.
  4. How I'd verify: Queue depth and age, Little's law: 2.9M items waiting at 400/s is about 2 hours of backlog; heap histogram.
  5. Root cause: Net growth of 400 jobs/s x 1,800 s = 720,000 in the first phase; unbounded queue hid the overload until the heap filled; long GC pauses made throughput worse and caused OOM kills that lost the queue.
  6. Fix: Bounded queue (for example 10,000) with rejection; durable queue (Kafka or SQS) for jobs that must survive; consumer concurrency limit tied to storage capacity; circuit breaker on storage; idempotency keys for retries.
  7. Prevention: Alert on queue age, load-test slow-dependency scenarios, retry budgets.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A durable queue changes guarantees to at-least-once and loosens ordering. I would not simply add consumers, which pushes more load onto the failing storage.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Jobs expire after 30 s -> Drop expired jobs at dequeue; processing them is wasted work.
  • Backlog is 2 hours; do you drain it? -> Prioritise fresh work, process the old backlog at a throttled rate or discard stale items.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a worker pool drained a 3-hour backlog of already-abandoned requests and starved new ones; adding deadlines to jobs fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more memory and consumers.
  • Hire: bounded queue, backpressure, durable spill, retries.
  • Strong hire: queue age metric, backlog math, expiry on dequeue, circuit breaker, idempotency.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing service on a 32-core host handles 480 ops/s at 8% CPU; adding threads does not help. Thread dumps taken 5 s apart show 28 of 32 threads BLOCKED on one monitor. A separate SQL counter for "orders today" is also slow under load (UPDATE stats SET orders = orders + 1 WHERE id = 1; with lock waits).

// shared cache guarded by one lock
synchronized (lock) {
    Price p = db.load(sku);          // 1.8 ms network call
    log.info("loaded {}", sku);      // 0.15 ms
    cache.put(sku, p);
}

Languages: Java, Kotlin

synchronized(lock) {
    val p = db.load(sku)             // 1.8 ms network call
    log.info("loaded {}", sku)       // 0.15 ms
    cache[sku] = p
}

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the thread pool." More threads queue on the same lock.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Read/write ratio? Is staleness acceptable? Is the SQL counter read often?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the DB call and the log out of the critical section; this alone is a small, safe change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Lock held across I/O (about 2 ms inside); global lock for a per-key resource; hot DB row.
  4. How I'd verify: Three jstack dumps, async-profiler lock mode or JFR; Postgres pg_locks with granted = false and wait_event.
  5. Root cause: The critical section takes about 2 ms, so max throughput is 1/0.002 = 500 ops/s regardless of cores, matching 480 ops/s. Amdahl: the serial part caps the speed-up.
  6. Fix: Do the load outside; only cache.put inside, or use ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent (per-bin locking) or a Caffeine loading cache, which also coalesces concurrent loads. Counter: shard into 16 rows (floor(random()*16)), sum on read, or increment in Redis and flush in batches, or insert event rows and aggregate.
  7. Prevention: Lock-wait metrics, code review rule that no I/O goes under a lock, load test by core count.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sharded counters make reads costlier and slightly stale. I would not switch to a lock-free structure without a measurement.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Reads dominate 99% -> ReadWriteLock/StampedLock or immutable copy-on-write snapshots.
  • Deadlock in a transfer between two accounts -> Acquire locks in a consistent order, use tryLock with timeout.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a log call inside a synchronized block capped a service at 500 ops/s on a 64-core box; moving it out gave a 40x gain.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds threads.
  • Hire: shortens the critical section, finds the 1/0.002 cap, shards the counter.
  • Strong hire: lock profiler evidence, Caffeine/computeIfAbsent coalescing, read-write trade-offs, deadlock ordering.

questions.promptHtml: How can a garbage-collection pause cause an outage in a distributed system that is otherwise healthy, and how do you prevent it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you connect runtime internals to cluster behavior such as false failure detection and leases.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A stop-the-world pause freezes the app. If it lasts longer than the health-check timeout, heartbeat interval or lock lease, the node looks dead: the load balancer ejects it, the cluster fails over, a lease expires and a second holder takes over, and the paused node wakes up believing it still owns something. That can cascade into retry storms or split brain. Prevention: pick a modern collector (G1 with a pause goal, or ZGC/Shenandoah for low pauses), size the heap right (a bigger heap with an old collector means longer pauses), reduce allocation, fix leaks, and keep timeouts above the worst realistic pause. Use fencing tokens for locks.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Young collections are frequent and short; full GCs on a large heap with older collectors can take seconds.
  • A leak raises old-gen occupancy; GCs become back-to-back and the JVM spends more than 98% of its time in GC ("GC overhead limit exceeded").
  • Containers: heap plus metaspace, threads and native memory must fit the pod limit or the OOM killer ends the process (verify flags such as -XX:MaxRAMPercentage for your JDK).
  • Allocation rate drives GC frequency: 1 GB/s allocation into a 2 GB young gen is a young GC every couple of seconds.
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms4g -Xmx4g -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime \
     -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -jar app.jar   # illustrative, tune with measurements

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Give it more heap" with a pausing collector.
  • Health-check or lease timeouts shorter than worst-case pauses.
  • Ignoring swap and container limits.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you detect a leak vs high allocation? -> Heap used after GC trending upward is a leak; high GC frequency with flat post-GC heap is allocation rate.
  2. Why do paused lock holders matter? -> They resume and write after the lease expired; fencing tokens let the store reject stale writes.
  3. When do you leave the JVM? -> Only for extreme latency or memory needs; it is a one-way door.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE tunes flags. Senior links pauses to false failure detection, sets timeouts relative to measured pauses, and uses fencing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: All nodes of a service performed a full GC within minutes of each other, were ejected by the load balancer, and the remaining nodes collapsed.

questions.contextHtml: A WebSocket gateway fleet (40 nodes, 2M concurrent mobile clients) must be restarted for a TLS library patch. The last restart caused 2M reconnects within 20 seconds, auth service CPU hit 100%, and 30% of clients saw errors for 12 minutes. Clients reconnect immediately on close with a fixed 1 s delay and no backoff. Reconnect handshake costs about 15 ms of auth CPU; the auth tier handles about 20,000 handshakes/s.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the rollout so it does not cause an outage, and fix the client behavior.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart at 3 AM." The herd is the same at any hour, and mobile clients are global.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can we ship a client update first? Can the server tell clients when to reconnect? Is auth cacheable (session resumption)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll nodes in small batches (for example 1 node = 50,000 clients) and wait until the reconnect wave drains; throttle handshakes at the gateway (token bucket) and return a retry-after.
  3. Hypotheses (why last time failed): Synchronised reconnects; no jitter; auth is the shared bottleneck.
  4. How I'd verify: Handshake rate and auth CPU during a canary node restart.
  5. Math: 2M clients at 20,000/s means at least 100 s even in a perfect spread; one node's 50,000 clients over 30 s is about 1,700/s, 8% of capacity. 40 nodes in sequence with a 60 s gap takes about 40 minutes.
  6. Fix: Server sends a close frame with a jittered reconnect-after (random across 0 to 120 s) before shutdown (graceful drain); client uses exponential backoff with full jitter and caps; connection rate limits; TLS session resumption and cached auth tokens to cut handshake cost.
  7. Prevention: Load test reconnect storms; alert on handshake rate; keep client backoff in the SDK rather than app code.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Longer drains delay the patch rollout; I accept that, and I would not restart all nodes at once to save time.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Old clients without backoff -> Server-side limits and a drain that spreads load with retry-after; force-upgrade over time.
  • Push notification wakes all devices at once -> Jitter push delivery and batch.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: after a failover all clients reconnected at once and the auth tier fell over; a per-client random delay on server-initiated closes made later restarts invisible.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restart at off-peak and hope.
  • Hire: batched rollout, jittered backoff, rate limits.
  • Strong hire: capacity math, graceful drain with reconnect-after, session resumption, load test.

questions.contextHtml: Your manager says: "The API is slow, p99 went from 250 ms to 1.4 s last week. We should double the pods." Data you can see: 60 pods, CPU at 30%, p50 unchanged at 40 ms, DB active connections at the max 100 with 40 clients waiting for a connection, one endpoint /search accounts for 85% of the p99 outliers, GC pauses average 25 ms. A deploy last Tuesday added a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in the order path.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond, and what do you investigate first? Use Amdahl's law in your answer.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Double the pods" (CPU is 30%, so more pods mean more DB connections and worse contention) or optimising code with no measurement.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which endpoints and which regions? When did it start relative to deploys? Is traffic up? What does the trace of a slow request show?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not scale pods blindly. If the pool is the bottleneck, cap per-pod pool size, shed low-priority load, or roll back the deploy if the timing matches.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) DB pool saturation with lock waits from the new FOR UPDATE; (2) a slow /search query (missing index or offset pagination); (3) GC (unlikely at 25 ms); (4) CPU (no, 30%).
  4. How I'd verify: USE on the pool (utilization 100%, saturation 40 waiting); pg_stat_activity wait events and pg_locks; EXPLAIN ANALYZE on /search; a slow-request trace.
  5. Root cause (to be confirmed): Resource saturation downstream, not app CPU. Amdahl: if 90% of time is in the DB, making app code 10x faster improves the total by only about 8%; adding pods increases DB connection demand.
  6. Fix: Fix the lock scope or query, add the right index, tune pool sizes, then re-measure p99 and queue depth.
  7. Prevention: Per-endpoint RED dashboards, pool wait metrics, deploy markers, slow query review in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not double pods; it costs money and can worsen DB contention. I would say that to the manager with the evidence.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Manager insists on scaling -> Do a time-boxed canary of 10 more pods and show p99 does not move.
  • /search is the main outlier but also low traffic -> Fix it anyway because it dominates the tail; check the weights by contribution.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team added pods three times during a slowdown; each increase added connections to the DB until it failed; the real cause was a missing index.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales out or optimises code blindly.
  • Hire: uses USE, finds pool saturation, checks the deploy.
  • Strong hire: communicates with evidence, uses Amdahl, plans a measured fix and a safe experiment.
